passage:
I'm Ujjwal. Elizabeth and I play the same block-building game in the computer lab after school.
On Tuesday a player called "SkyKing" kept messaging her. First he said her castle was cool. Then he asked which school she went to. Then: "Don't tell anyone we talk, okay?"
Elizabeth went quiet. She stopped typing and stared at the screen for a long time. Then she took a screenshot, blocked him, and walked straight over to Mr Pinto.
Mr Pinto read it, thanked her, and said she'd done exactly right. He reported the account and phoned her mother before we left.

qa.q: What did SkyKing ask after saying her castle was cool?
qa.a: Which school she went to.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth have been feeling when she stared at the screen?
qa.a: Elizabeth probably felt uneasy and suspicious, especially when SkyKing asked her to keep it secret.

qa.q: Which steps did Elizabeth take that others could copy?
qa.a: She didn't share her school, took a screenshot, blocked the account and told a trusted adult straight away.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see what Elizabeth did?
qa.a: Ujjwal can't be sure what she was feeling, but sees her go quiet and then act fast and calmly.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl refuse to share details with a secretive online contact and report it.

passage:
Before: On Monday, Sumit posted a photo in his school uniform on a gaming site, the badge clearly showing. A stranger commented, "Nice! Which area is your school in?"
During: On Wednesday, the same person messaged: "Send your address, I'll send you free game coins. Keep it between us." Sumit's stomach turned. He didn't reply. That evening he showed the messages to his father, Lalit.
Lalit didn't shout. He said, "Thank you for telling me." Together they blocked and reported the account and deleted the uniform photo.
After: On Saturday, Sumit changed his profile picture to a drawing of a tiger. "Only friends I know can see my posts now," he said.

qa.q: What was clearly showing in Sumit's uniform photo?
qa.a: The school badge.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when his stomach turned?
qa.a: Sumit felt uneasy and scared, sensing that the offer and the secrecy were not right.

qa.q: What did Sumit and Lalit do that made him safer?
qa.a: They blocked and reported the account, deleted the photo, and Sumit made his posts visible only to friends he knows.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel when Sumit shows him the messages?
qa.a: Lalit is probably worried but grateful that Sumit told him, which is why he stays calm and says thank you.

grounding: Over a week a child learns to protect his details and tells his father about a pressuring contact.

passage:
Gurleen, come, sit. You're asking why I fuss about your tablet. Let me tell you about when I was eleven.
Back then, there was an internet café near our school. I used to go to a chat room about cricket. One man there was very friendly. He knew everything about cricket. After a week, he asked for my phone number and said, "Don't tell your parents, they won't understand."
That word, "don't tell," made my ears go hot. I logged off. I walked home and told my mother that same evening.
She called the café owner, who banned that account from the café computers.
That is why your Jeevan mama asks questions.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan go to use the chat room?
qa.a: An internet café near his school.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when his ears went hot?
qa.a: Jeevan felt alarmed and uneasy, because the man asked him to keep a secret from his parents.

qa.q: What choice did the eleven-year-old Jeevan make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He logged off and told his mother that same evening, which ended the contact and brought in a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's mother have felt when he told her?
qa.a: She was probably worried but glad he told her quickly, which is why she acted and called the café owner.

grounding: An uncle recalls refusing a secretive online contact as a child and telling his mother.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage:
The cyber café in the town had only three computers. Imran typed "how to make crops grow fast" for his school project.
The first result had a shiny picture: "MIRACLE POWDER! Double your harvest in a week!"
"Look, Kiran didi! We should tell Abba."
His sister leaned over. "See that small word above it? 'Sponsored.' Someone paid to put it there."
"But it's the first one."
"Being first doesn't mean true." She scrolled down to a page from the agriculture university about soil and water.
Imran read it, frowning. "It doesn't say a week."
"Real farming never does."

qa.q: What small word did Kiran point to above the first result?
qa.a: 'Sponsored.'

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he wanted to tell Abba about the powder?
qa.a: Imran felt excited and hopeful, believing the advert's promise.

qa.q: What could Imran check next time he searches?
qa.a: He could look for the 'Sponsored' label and compare with a reliable source, like the university page.

qa.q: How does Kiran see the miracle powder advert?
qa.a: Kiran sees it as a paid advert making big promises, not a trustworthy fact.

grounding: In a small-town cyber café, a child learns to spot sponsored results and look for reliable sources.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage:
In their Cape Town classroom, Paulo and Lindiwe were researching the fastest animal for a poster.
Paulo found a video: "The FASTEST animal ever — a secret the scientists hide!" It said a lizard could outrun a car.
"Wow! Let's write that," said Paulo.
Lindiwe frowned. "Who made the video?"
They checked. It was a channel that also sold lizard toys, and it didn't say where the fact came from.
Lindiwe searched a museum website. It said the peregrine falcon, diving.
"So the lizard thing was made up?"
"Maybe just to get views," said Lindiwe.
Paulo crossed out "lizard" on the poster, a bit sulky. "The falcon's cooler anyway."

qa.q: What did the museum website say was the fastest animal?
qa.a: The peregrine falcon, diving.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling while crossing out "lizard"?
qa.a: Paulo felt a bit sulky and disappointed that the exciting fact was wrong.

qa.q: What questions helped Lindiwe judge the video?
qa.a: Lindiwe asked who made it, noticed they sold lizard toys, and saw it gave no source, then checked a museum site.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe see videos with headlines like "secret the scientists hide"?
qa.a: Lindiwe is wary of them and thinks they may be made to get views rather than to tell the truth.

grounding: Two children in South Africa check a sensational video against a reliable source.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage:
In the school computer lab, Jahnavi and Neelam were searching for healthy snacks for a project.
A bright box popped up: "Drink GrowMax juice and grow taller like a champion!" There was a boy dunking a basketball.
"Should we put it in?" asked Neelam.
Jahnavi pointed. "It says 'Ad' in the corner. And it's selling the juice."
"But it has a doctor in a white coat."
"Anyone can wear a white coat in an ad."
They asked the teacher, who showed them the government nutrition page. Nothing about magic juice.
Neelam closed the ad box with a firm click. "Fooled me for a second."

qa.q: What did the ad show?
qa.a: A boy dunking a basketball.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she said "Fooled me for a second"?
qa.a: Neelam felt a bit embarrassed but also relieved to have spotted the trick.

qa.q: What clues helped Jahnavi spot that it was an ad?
qa.a: The 'Ad' label in the corner and the fact that it was selling the juice, plus knowing that a white coat doesn't prove anything.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Jahnavi and Neelam's question?
qa.a: The teacher is likely pleased that they questioned the ad and asked for help finding a reliable source.

grounding: Two children in a school computer lab spot an ad pretending to be health advice.

passage:
In their flat in Istanbul, Elif played her racing game under the blanket until almost midnight. The next morning she yawned through maths and missed an easy question. At football, she tripped twice.
Her brother Sami found her dozing on the sofa after school. "You're a zombie."
"I'm fine," she mumbled.
That evening, the new level unlocked. Elif's thumb hovered over the button. She looked at her bag, still packed with homework, and at the football by the door.
She put the tablet on the kitchen shelf. "Sami, don't let me take it to bed."
"Deal," said Sami. "Want to kick the ball first?"

qa.q: Where did Elif put the tablet?
qa.a: On the kitchen shelf.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling when her thumb hovered over the button?
qa.a: Elif felt tempted and torn between the new level and her homework and football.

qa.q: Which choice helped Elif, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the tablet in the kitchen at night took away the temptation, so she could sleep and do her homework.

qa.q: How does Sami see Elif's tiredness?
qa.a: Sami notices she's like a "zombie" and supports her plan by agreeing not to let her take the tablet to bed.

grounding: A child in Turkey notices late-night gaming is hurting her day and sets a limit.

passage:
At the school hostel, lights-out was at nine. Hansa lay under her blanket watching funny videos on her phone, the screen lighting up her face.
At eleven, Jagdish Sir, the warden, knocked softly and shone his torch. "Phone, please."
Hansa handed it over, cheeks hot.
The next morning she fell asleep in the library. At kabaddi practice she was slow.
That evening, Jagdish Sir sat with her in the common room. "Games and videos are fine. But sleep is when your body grows and your brain sorts the day. What if you watch after dinner, and I keep the phone at night?"
Hansa thought, then nodded. "Only after dinner."

qa.q: What time was lights-out at the hostel?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she handed over the phone?
qa.a: Hansa felt embarrassed at being caught.

qa.q: What plan did Jagdish Sir suggest, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: He suggested watching after dinner and keeping the phone at night, which keeps fun time but protects sleep.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Sir feel when Hansa agrees?
qa.a: Jagdish Sir probably feels relieved that she accepted a fair plan instead of arguing.

grounding: A hostel warden helps a child balance videos with sleep and activity.

passage:
I'm Karthik, Sangeeta's brother. Last summer, she was stuck on a farming game on Amma's phone. Every morning she'd grab it before brushing her teeth.
Then the colony boys started a cricket match in the evenings. The first day she said no. The second day she watched from the balcony, the phone still in her hand.
On the third day she left the phone on the charger and came down. She was a terrible bowler. But she came back sweaty and laughing, and slept early.
After that, she played her game only in the afternoon. I don't know if she planned it, but it seemed to work.

qa.q: What game was Sangeeta stuck on?
qa.a: A farming game.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been feeling when she watched from the balcony?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably felt curious and tempted to join, but still pulled by the game.

qa.q: What could help Sangeeta keep the balance she found?
qa.a: Keeping her game time to the afternoon and making sure evenings stay for outdoor play.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Sangeeta's change?
qa.a: Karthik isn't sure if she planned it, but sees her play outside, sleep earlier and use the game less.

grounding: A sibling watches a child shift from a phone game to outdoor play and better sleep.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage:
Last year, I used to ask the voice assistant on Papa's phone everything. It sounded so sure that I thought it knew it all.
Then for my science homework I asked, "How many legs does a spider have?" It said six. I wrote six.
My friend Bhavna said, "Spiders have eight. Insects have six." We checked the textbook. She was right.
I felt stupid. Then I felt annoyed at the phone. I even said, "You're wrong," and it just said, "Sorry, I didn't catch that."
That's when I understood: it doesn't know anything, it just finds things. And it doesn't feel sorry. Now I check the book too.
— Deepak

qa.q: How many legs did the voice assistant say a spider has?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he found out the answer was wrong?
qa.a: Deepak felt foolish at first and then annoyed at the phone for sounding so sure.

qa.q: What habit did Deepak take from this, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Deepak now checks the textbook too, because the assistant can be wrong.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see the voice assistant after this?
qa.a: Bhavna probably sees it as a tool that can make mistakes, not something to trust over the book.

grounding: A child recalls learning that a voice assistant can be wrong and does not really feel.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage:
Class 5 teacher's note.
During project time, Lokesh and Ayesha used the class chatbot to find the capital of Australia. It said "Sydney." Ayesha said, "I think it's Canberra," but Lokesh said, "The computer can't be wrong."
I asked them to check the atlas. Canberra.
Lokesh looked shocked. Then he typed, "Why did you lie?" The chatbot replied, "I'm sorry for the confusion."
"It said sorry, so it feels bad," Lokesh said.
We talked about how it's a program that puts words together, not a person with feelings, and that it can be wrong. Tomorrow I'll have the class check three chatbot answers against books. — Ms Ghosh

qa.q: What did the chatbot say was the capital of Australia?
qa.a: Sydney.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he found out the chatbot was wrong?
qa.a: Lokesh felt shocked and a little betrayed, because he believed the computer couldn't be wrong.

qa.q: What does Ms Ghosh plan next, and how does it help?
qa.a: She plans for the class to check three chatbot answers against books, so they learn to verify what it says.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see the chatbot's answer?
qa.a: Ayesha trusts her own knowledge enough to question it, showing she doesn't treat the chatbot as always right.

grounding: A teacher notes children learning that a chatbot can be wrong and does not truly feel.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage:
Dear Diary,
Today I was sad because nobody picked me for the relay team. At home I typed it into the chat app's robot helper. It said, "That sounds hard. You are amazing and deserve to be picked!"
It felt nice for a minute. Then I thought: it doesn't even know me. It said "amazing" but it hasn't seen me run.
I told Tanuja didi. She said, "The robot just writes nice sentences. It doesn't care like a person does. I care, though." Then she took me to the park to practise baton passing.
I'm faster already. And didi actually laughed at my jokes.
— Ira

qa.q: Why was Ira sad today?
qa.a: Because nobody picked Ira for the relay team.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling on noticing the robot didn't know Ira at all?
qa.a: Ira felt doubtful and a little let down, noticing the robot's kind words were empty.

qa.q: Which response helped Ira more, and why?
qa.a: Tanuja didi's did, because she really listened and helped Ira practise, which a program can't do.

qa.q: How does Tanuja didi see the robot helper?
qa.a: Tanuja didi sees it as something that writes nice sentences but doesn't truly care the way a person does.

grounding: In her diary a child notices that a chatbot's comfort is not real caring.

passage:
In the school bus queue in Chennai, Yamini shoved Nilesh from behind and laughed. His water bottle fell and rolled into the gutter.
Nilesh swung round, fists tight. Yamini grinned, waiting.
He stopped. He counted in his head: one, two, three, four, five. His breathing slowed a little.
"That wasn't funny," he said, voice shaking. "Pick up my bottle, or I'm telling the conductor."
Yamini's grin slipped. She rolled her eyes but fished the bottle out.
Nilesh took it and got on the bus. His hands were still trembling, but he hadn't hit anyone.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh's water bottle roll?
qa.a: Into the gutter.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he swung round with fists tight?
qa.a: Nilesh felt angry and humiliated after being shoved and laughed at.

qa.q: What did pausing to count to five give Nilesh the chance to do?
qa.a: It gave him time to calm down enough to use firm words instead of his fists.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Nilesh's response?
qa.a: Yamini expected a fight and seemed surprised when he stayed calm and firm, which took the fun out of her joke.

grounding: A child pauses and counts before responding to a shove, choosing words over hitting.

passage:
"Your drawing looks like a baby did it," Rashmi said, loud enough for the whole playground to hear.
Nazia's hand tightened on the paper. "Take that back."
"Why? It's true."
Nazia took a step forward. Then she stopped. She turned and walked to the water tap and splashed her face.
When she came back, Rashmi was still there. "Running away?"
"No," said Nazia. "I'm choosing not to fight. What you said was mean. It hurt."
Rashmi opened her mouth, then shut it. "Fine. Whatever."
Nazia smoothed the drawing and went to show her teacher.

qa.q: Where did Nazia go after she stopped?
qa.a: To the water tap.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when her hand tightened on the paper?
qa.a: Nazia felt angry and hurt by Rashmi's mean comment.

qa.q: Which choice by Nazia worked, and why?
qa.a: Walking away to splash her face gave her time to cool down, so she could tell Rashmi calmly that it hurt instead of fighting.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi react differently than expected?
qa.a: Rashmi was ready for a fight, so Nazia calmly naming the hurt left her with nothing to say.

grounding: On a playground a child walks away to cool down, then answers an insult with words.

passage:
I still remember the day Baljeet knocked my tiffin off the table in Class 5. My rajma went everywhere. He laughed and said, "Oops."
I wanted to throw my bottle at him. My arm was already up.
But I put it down. I walked to the sink and washed my hands slowly, counting the tiles. Twelve.
When I came back, I said, "Baljeet, that was my lunch. Say sorry and help clean it."
He looked surprised. He said sorry, and even gave me half his parathas.
If I'd thrown the bottle, I'd be the one in trouble. I'm Madhuri, and I'm still a little proud of that day.

qa.q: What did Madhuri count at the sink?
qa.a: The tiles, twelve of them.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when her arm was already up?
qa.a: Madhuri felt furious and wanted to hurt Baljeet back.

qa.q: What did Madhuri's pause at the sink allow her to do?
qa.a: It gave her time to calm down so she could ask for an apology and help instead of throwing her bottle.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when Madhuri came back calm?
qa.a: Baljeet was surprised, and Madhuri's calm, firm words likely made him feel sorry enough to share his parathas.

grounding: A young person recalls pausing before hitting back and using words instead.

passage:
The night before the block-level science exam, Vishal couldn't eat. In the courtyard of their house in the kasba, he kept flipping pages.
"My heart is going fast," he told his sister Pooja. "What if I forget everything?"
Pooja sat beside him on the charpai. "That's your body getting ready. Let's slow it down. Breathe in for four, hold, out for four."
They did it five times. Vishal's shoulders came down a little.
"Now close the book. Tell me three things you know about plants."
He told her four.
The next morning, at the exam hall door, Pooja saw him breathe in for four, then walk in.

qa.q: What exam was Vishal worried about?
qa.a: The block-level science exam.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he said his heart was going fast?
qa.a: Vishal felt anxious and scared that he would forget everything.

qa.q: How can Vishal use what Pooja taught him in other exams?
qa.a: He can do the slow four-count breathing before starting and remind himself of things he already knows.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Vishal's racing heart?
qa.a: Pooja sees it as his body getting ready, not a sign that he will fail.

grounding: In a small town, a child learns a breathing routine to handle exam nerves.

passage:
The music school in Seoul was very quiet before the spring recital. Soo-ah sat backstage, her fingers cold, pressing imaginary keys on her knees.
"My hands are shaking," she whispered to Tomas, who was playing after her.
"Mine too. Watch." Tomas pressed his palms together hard, then let go. "Squeeze, then relax. Five times."
Soo-ah tried it. Her hands felt warmer.
"Now think of the first four notes only," Tomas said. "Not the whole piece."
When her name was called, Soo-ah walked out, sat, took one breath, and played the first four notes. Then the next ones followed.

qa.q: What did Tomas tell Soo-ah to think of?
qa.a: The first four notes only.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling as she pressed imaginary keys on her knees?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt nervous; her hands were cold and shaking before the recital.

qa.q: Which calming steps helped Soo-ah, and why?
qa.a: Squeezing and relaxing her hands warmed and calmed them, and focusing on four notes made the piece feel manageable.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel while sharing his trick?
qa.a: Tomas is nervous too, but helping Soo-ah may make him feel steadier and less alone.

grounding: A child in Korea uses a hand-squeeze routine and small focus to manage recital nerves.

passage:
In the school auditorium, Rukmini waited in the wings for her Tamil poem recitation. Her mouth was dry. She kept whispering the first line.
Shankar, the boy from her class who went on after her, noticed. "You okay?"
"I'll forget," she said.
"Do the thing Ma'am taught us. Feet flat, look at one spot on the back wall, slow breath."
Rukmini pressed her feet into the floor. She found the clock on the back wall. Breathed.
When she walked out, she looked at the clock, not the faces. Her voice wobbled on the first line, then settled.
Afterwards, Shankar gave her a thumbs up.

qa.q: What did Rukmini look at instead of the faces?
qa.a: The clock on the back wall.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when her mouth was dry?
qa.a: Rukmini was very nervous and afraid she would forget her poem.

qa.q: What calming routine helped Rukmini, and how could she use it again?
qa.a: Feet flat, looking at one spot and slow breathing helped; she can use it before any performance or test.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Rukmini finishes?
qa.a: Shankar is probably happy for her and glad he reminded her of the routine 👍.

grounding: A child uses a grounding routine to handle nerves before a recitation.

passage:
At school in Amman, a boy flicked Sami's ear in the corridor. "Dumbo! Can you fly with those?"
Some kids laughed. Sami pulled his hat down over his ears and walked faster.
At home, he stood in front of the mirror, pressing his ears flat.
His friend Layla came over with homework. She saw him. "What are you doing?"
"My ears are too big."
"Says who? That boy with the loud mouth?" Layla shrugged. "You have the best laugh in class. That's what I notice."
Sami let go of his ears. The next day he didn't pull his hat down, even when the boy looked.

qa.q: What did Sami pull down over his ears?
qa.a: His hat.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling when he pressed his ears flat in the mirror?
qa.a: Sami felt ashamed and hurt, as if the teasing had made his ears something to hide.

qa.q: How did Layla help, and what else could help Sami?
qa.a: Layla reminded him the comment came from a loud, unkind boy and named something she liked; a teacher could also be told if it continues.

qa.q: How does Layla see Sami?
qa.a: Layla sees his great laugh, not his ears, and doesn't think the teasing is true.

grounding: A child in Jordan is teased about his ears and regains self-respect with a friend's support.

passage:

passage:
I'm Aadhya, and I sit behind Tenzin. Last week, a girl pinched his cheek and said, "Look at these round cheeks! Like a momo!"
Everyone laughed, and I laughed too, for a second. Tenzin didn't.
He was quiet the whole lesson. At lunch, he didn't eat his tiffin.
Then, the next morning, when the same girl said it again, Tenzin looked at her and said, "Please stop. I don't like jokes about my face."
She said, "It was just a joke." He said, "Not to me," and turned back to his book.
I felt bad that I'd laughed. I told him sorry at break.

qa.q: What did the girl compare Tenzin's cheeks to?
qa.a: A momo.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have been feeling when he didn't eat his tiffin?
qa.a: Tenzin probably felt hurt and self-conscious after being laughed at.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do that kept his self-respect?

qa.q: How does Aadhya see her own laugh?

passage:
I'm Eshaan. At the Wednesday break, a group of boys circled a new kid near the water cooler, copying his accent and grabbing his cap.
Some of our class were laughing and filming. Amandeep, my friend, was standing next to me. I saw his jaw go tight.
He didn't laugh. He didn't film. He walked off quickly. I thought he was leaving.
He came back two minutes later with Mrs Reddy, the duty teacher. She told the group to hand back the cap and delete the videos, and took the new kid to the office to talk.
Later I heard that Mrs Reddy called all the parents that afternoon.

qa.q: What were the boys copying?
qa.a: The new kid's accent.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have been feeling when his jaw went tight?
qa.a: Amandeep probably felt angry and uncomfortable seeing the new kid mocked.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that others could copy?
qa.a: He refused to laugh or film and went straight to fetch the duty teacher.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see what Amandeep did?
qa.a: Eshaan first thought Amandeep was leaving, then saw that he went to get help instead of watching.

grounding: A friend watches a boy refuse to join in bullying and fetch a teacher.

passage:

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when his stomach felt heavy?

passage:
Irawati, you're asking what to do about the girls who tease your friend. Let me tell you what happened when I was your age.
There was a boy in my class called Sunder. He stammered. Every day, three boys made fun of him. The others laughed. I laughed too, at first.
One day I saw him crying behind the school wall. That night I couldn't sleep. The next morning, before class, I went to the headmaster and told him everything.
The headmaster called the three boys in that same morning and spoke to their parents. He moved Sunder to sit with me.
We stayed friends for forty years. That is your Yusuf nana's story.

qa.q: How many boys made fun of Sunder every day?
qa.a: Three boys.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling the night he couldn't sleep?
qa.a: Yusuf felt guilty and troubled after seeing Sunder crying.

qa.q: What choice did young Yusuf make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He went to the headmaster the next morning and told everything, which got an adult to stop the teasing.

qa.q: How might Sunder have felt when the headmaster moved him to sit with Yusuf?
qa.a: Sunder probably felt relieved and less alone, with a friend beside him.

grounding: A grandfather tells how he stopped laughing at bullying and reported it.

passage:
"Climb the water tank ladder. Top rung. I dare you," said Farhan.
Karthik looked up. The ladder was rusty and very high.
"No way. It's dangerous."
"Scared?"
"Yes. And so should you be." Karthik grinned. "Race you to the ground instead. Loser buys the next bat."
Farhan hesitated. "You're boring."
"And alive."
Farhan laughed. "Fine. But I'm winning."
They ran. At home that evening, Karthik told his father about the rusty ladder. His father called the society secretary right away to have it chained.

qa.q: What was the ladder like?
qa.a: Rusty and very high.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he looked up at the ladder?
qa.a: Karthik felt scared and wary, knowing the climb was dangerous.

qa.q: How did Karthik say no without losing Farhan as a friend?
qa.a: He admitted he was scared, joked, and offered a fun race instead, so they could still play together.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Karthik says "And alive"?
qa.a: Farhan probably feels amused and a bit relieved, since the joke let him drop the dare without losing face.

grounding: A child refuses a dangerous dare with humour and his father makes the ladder safe.

passage:
Last year, in Class 6, Pranav dared me to ring Mrs D'Souza's doorbell and run. She's old and walks with a stick.
"Everyone's done it," he said. "Don't be a baby."
I felt my face heat. I wanted to be brave. But I kept thinking of Mrs D'Souza getting up slowly, walking to the door, and finding nobody.
"No," I said. "That's mean to her."
Pranav rolled his eyes. For a day he didn't talk to me. Then he came over with his cricket bat like nothing had happened.
I'm Bhavna. I still wave to Mrs D'Souza every morning. She always waves back.

qa.q: Whose doorbell did Pranav dare Bhavna to ring?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza's.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when her face heated?
qa.a: Bhavna felt embarrassed and pressured, wanting to look brave in front of Pranav.

qa.q: What helped Bhavna say no?
qa.a: Thinking about how the dare would affect Mrs D'Souza made it clear that it was unkind.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt when Bhavna refused?
qa.a: Pranav was probably annoyed and embarrassed for a day, but still valued the friendship enough to come back.

grounding: A young person recalls refusing an unkind dare and keeping the friendship.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Thursday.
At lunch today, Kalyani dared Ritu to jump off the top of the school wall onto the sandpit. Ritu looked at the height, then said, "No. I'll break my leg. Let's do long jump on the ground instead."
Kalyani laughed and said, "Chicken!" Ritu didn't budge. She drew a line in the sand and said, "Beat me."
They ended up playing long jump for the rest of lunch.
Afterwards, Ritu came to me and told me about the dare. I thanked her. This afternoon I spoke to Kalyani and to the class about wall-jumping, and asked the caretaker to put up a sign. — Ms Nair

qa.q: What did Kalyani dare Ritu to jump off?
qa.a: The top of the school wall.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she looked at the height?
qa.a: Ritu felt afraid of getting hurt, but steady enough to refuse.

qa.q: Which part of Ritu's refusal kept the friendship going?
qa.a: She offered a safer game instead, long jump on the ground, so they could still play together.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel after the long jump game?
qa.a: Kalyani probably had fun and may see that Ritu can be brave in a safe way.

grounding: A teacher's note records a child refusing a risky dare and offering a safer game.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage:
In Copenhagen, Emil's group had to build a bridge from paper straws. Emil was the leader. He had a plan, but it kept collapsing.
Sofia, who hardly spoke, tapped the table. "What if we make triangles? They're stronger."
Emil hesitated. It wasn't his idea. Then he said, "Let's try it."
The triangle bridge held twenty coins.
When the teacher asked who had the winning idea, Emil could have said "our team." Instead he said, "Sofia thought of the triangles."
Sofia turned pink, but she smiled. Emil felt a small tug of envy, then something better.

qa.q: How many coins did the triangle bridge hold?
qa.a: Twenty coins.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling when he hesitated?
qa.a: Emil felt a bit reluctant and envious because the idea wasn't his.

qa.q: Which choice by Emil made him a good leader?
qa.a: He tried Sofia's idea and gave her the credit clearly, instead of taking it for the team or himself.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel when Emil names her?
qa.a: Sofia feels shy but proud and valued, knowing her quiet idea was recognised.

grounding: A group leader in Denmark gives credit to a quiet teammate's idea.

subtype: Roles in Group Tasks & Sharing Credit
passage:
In the school science fair hall, Himani's team stood by their water filter model. Himani had organised everything: who did what, when.
The judge asked, "Who designed the charcoal layer?"
Himani opened her mouth to answer. Then she looked at Neelam, who was quietly wiping the jar.
"Neelam did," Himani said. "She found it in a library book and tested three kinds of charcoal."
Neelam looked up, startled. The judge asked her questions, and she answered clearly.
Later, Neelam said, "Thanks. I didn't think anyone noticed."
"I noticed," said Himani.

qa.q: What did Neelam test for the charcoal layer?
qa.a: Three kinds of charcoal.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she looked up, startled?
qa.a: Neelam felt surprised, having thought no one noticed her work.

qa.q: What could Himani keep doing as a team leader?
qa.a: She can keep noticing quiet members' work and naming it, so everyone feels part of the team.

qa.q: How does the judge see Neelam after Himani speaks?
qa.a: The judge sees Neelam as the one who knows the charcoal part and asks her directly.

grounding: A team leader at a science fair credits a quiet teammate's work.

passage:
I'm Kishore. Our team won the inter-house quiz last week. Lalit was the captain.
During the quiz, Lalit mostly listened. He let me answer the sports questions, and let Priyamvada do science. When he didn't know, he said so.
When the principal gave him the trophy and asked him to say something, Lalit said, "Priyamvada got the hardest one. Kishore got four in a row. I just pressed the buzzer."
Everyone laughed. I felt my ears go hot.
I don't know if Lalit planned that speech. But the whole team walked back together, passing the trophy around.

qa.q: How many answers did Kishore get in a row?
qa.a: Four in a row.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when his ears went hot?
qa.a: Kishore felt surprised and proud to be named in front of everyone.

qa.q: What made Lalit a good captain in this quiz?
qa.a: He shared roles by strength, admitted what he didn't know, and gave credit to teammates publicly.

qa.q: How might Priyamvada see Lalit's speech?
qa.a: Priyamvada probably feels appreciated, since Lalit named her hard answer first.

grounding: A teammate watches a quiz captain share roles and credit fairly.
